catalog_quote: A phonological word in Ibaloy can only have one primary stress which is either penultimate or final. Since stress assignment takes into account the shape of the root syllable template and its phonemic content, it is best described in relation to the various root types. ... Root stress in Ibaloy is predictable. ... With roots of one syllable, stress automatically falls on that syllable. With roots of two or more syllables, stress is placed on the first syllable of the root, if is open and if it does not contain the vowel /a/. When the first syllable is closed or contains the vowel /a/, the second syllable receives stress. Then every second syllable from the first one stressed also receives stress. Since a phonological word can only have one primary stress, it follows that the rightmost stress is primary, and the other is secondary. ... Disyllabic roots: these roots receive penultimate pr…

(2) Deciding source: a 615-pp. 2004 ANU PhD thesis that is the sole grammar-level description of Ibaloy in Glottolog, with a dedicated phonology part and explicit stress analysis from the author's own fieldwork; nothing newer or more specialised (no phonology article, JIPA Illustration, instrumental study) was found via Crossref, the SIL [ibl] archive listing (23 items), archive.org or MPG PuRe. sources.citation: Walrod, Michael R. (2006). The marker is the message: the influence of discourse markers and particles on textual meaning.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: A 10-ICAL discourse paper on discourse markers and particles across northern Philippine languages (mostly Ga'dang and Ilocano). 'Prosody' in it means 'semantic prosody' of discourse particles, not phonological stress. No phonology section; it says nothing about where Ibaloi word stress falls. Glottolog's 'grammar sketch' tag for Ibaloy is a mislabel: the paper contains one short list of four Ibaloi particles and nothing else on the language.

sources.citation: Scheerer, Otto. 1905. The Nabaloi Dialect. (Ethnological Survey Publications II/2.) Manila: Bureau of Public Printing. 115 pp. [archive.org item atf7591.0001.001.umich.edu, scanned text; MPG PuRe item_403669 PDF is access-restricted]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No word-accent rule stated. The pronunciation section treats segment values only; the four scanned hits for 'accent' concern sentence emphasis (choice of construction 'decided by the accent the speaker is laying') and rhythm in a children's rhyme. Accents are marked ad hoc on some transcribed words but no placement generalisation is given. scanned quality is poor, so a short remark could have been missed, but nothing resembling a stress rule surfaced.
sources.locator: 'The Nabaloi alphabet / Pronunciation' and 'Signs employed' sections (scanned lines ~940-1345); a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/syllable/penult
